title: Exertional rhabdomyolysis and acute renal failure in marathon runners
population: Review of case reports of exertional rhabdomyolysis and acute renal failure in marathon runners
findings: Strenuous exercise, including marathon running, can damage skeletal muscle cells (exertional rhabdomyolysis); in most cases the damage resolves without consequence (abstract).

When the damage is profound, muscle proteins are released into the blood; myoglobin in high concentration, under conditions such as dehydration and heat stress, can precipitate in the kidneys and cause acute renal failure (abstract).

Acute renal failure in marathon runners is relatively infrequent; case reports show a high proportion had taken analgesics, had a viral or bacterial infection, or had a pre-existing condition (abstract).
The author describes the rare cases as a perfect storm of heat stress, dehydration, latent myopathy, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory or other analgesic use and infection coming together (abstract).
limitations: Narrative review resting on case reports, so it gives no frequency among runners. The abstract does not describe the signs a runner would notice (dark urine, severe muscle pain), so the warning-signs list takes from it the link between severe muscle damage after a hard effort and kidney injury; the signs themselves are common clinical description that this record does not quote.
implications: Supports a clinician-level sign for very dark or scant urine with severe muscle pain after a hard or long effort, with a line telling the clinician about heat and any painkillers taken; the engine states no frequency.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, journal, year, author and DOI, with no correction notice; Europe PMC abstract (PMID 17465608) read on 2026-11-13 and each finding is stated in it. Task WS1.
